newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy needs to act on spending in EMU bid - IMF.
newsitem.headline: Italy needs to act on spending in EMU bid - IMF.

text.p: Membership of European monetary union is within Italy's reach, but the government must display firm leadership and introduce structural reforms on state spending, the International Monetary Fund said in a report.

However the IMF said that Italy's public sector deficit would overshoot in 1996 and added that the deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio in 1997 would be 3.75 percent against a government target of 3.1 percent.

"On the basis of the information available to date, we would estimate that...the state sector deficit...will be in the order of 133 trillion lire (7.1 percent of GDP)," the IMF said in its preliminary survey on Italy following a visit by IMF experts.

The survey said the overrun in 1996 state accounts was due in part to inadequate returns from some budget measures along with poor expenditure control, especially at a local government level and in the autonomous agencies.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government has introduced a 62.5 trillion lire deficit cutting budget for 1997 in a bid to bring the deficit/GDP ratio near to the three percent level demanded by the Maastricht Treaty.

The IMF welcomed the budget but said it failed "to provide assurance both for the achievement of the 1997 target itself and its sustainability thereafter". It added that economic growth next year would be slower than envisaged but said interest rates would be lower than the government was predicting.
Taking this into consideration, along with the 1996 deficit overshoot, the deficit/GDP ratio would be some 3.75 percent next year, the IMF predicted.
"We call for the definition, as early as possible in 1997, of durable cost-saving measures affecting spending on social security, health and public employment," the survey said.

It said that a 1995 reform of the state pensions system was being phased in too slowly and added that pensioners should start to pay some health contributions. It also called for a strict enforcement of a hiring freeze in the state sector.

"While the bulk of the correction must be on expenditure cuts, it is possible that these may not yield sufficient immediate savings to secure the 1997 target. Any action on the revenue side should, however, firmly avoid further increases in an already excessive burden of direction taxation," it said.
It said its forecasts were based on the assumption that the European Union would accept several accounting changes included in the 1997 budget.
If these were rejected, an even larger corrective package would be needed early next year to meet 1997 goals.

"If the political will and majority required to enact it cannot be mustered, the only remaining course of action will be to concentrate on credibly achieving the Maastricht criteria in 1998," the IMF said.
But if structural measures were introduced in early 1997, then Italy could "maintain a budget deficit of just under three percent of GDP in the period beyond 1997", the IMF said.
It warned the government that inaction on the spending front could prove disastrous.

"We would note that the government's decision that Italy should strive to join EMU from the start has substantially raised the stakes, amplifying not only the payoffs for success but also the penalties for failure," the survey said.
It noted that market rates had fallen substantially in recent months as investors bet that Italy would win its EMU battle.

"But to the extent that they reflect 'convergence plays' by market participants, they run the risk of unraveling...any such development in 1997-98 would prove extremely costly," the report said. -- Rome newsroom +396 6782501
